## Overview

- Precise knowledge of the architecture of the liver, biliary tract, and pancreas is essential
- Understanding related blood vessels and lymphatic drainage is critical for hepatopancreatobiliary surgical operations
- This chapter covers:
  - **Liver anatomy** — external and functional (segmental)
  - **Biliary tract** — intrahepatic and extrahepatic anatomy
  - **Pancreas** — structure, ductal system, and anomalies
  - **Vascular anatomy** — hepatic artery, portal vein, and variations
  - **Lymphatic drainage and nerve supply**

## External Anatomy of the Liver

- The liver lies protected under the lower ribs, closely applied to the undersurface of the diaphragm
- Most of the liver bulk lies **to the right of the midline**
- The lower border lies near the right costal margin
- Extends as a wedge to the left of the midline, between the stomach and left dome of the diaphragm

**Surfaces:**
- **Upper surface**: boldly convex, molded to the diaphragm
- **Undersurface**: concave, extends down to a sharp anterior border
- **Posterior surface**: triangular in outline with its base to the right

## Peritoneal Attachments and Ligaments

- The liver is invested with **peritoneum** except on the posterior surface
- **Falciform ligament**: attaches liver to anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm
- **Left and right triangular ligaments**: formed where peritoneum reflects onto the diaphragm
- **Bare area**: liver tissue devoid of peritoneum between the "leaves" of the triangular ligaments
- **Ligamentum teres** (round ligament): remnant of obliterated umbilical vein, runs through umbilical fissure
- **Ligamentum venosum**: remnant of ductus venosus, lies in fissure separating caudate lobe

## Surface Projections and Relations

- Upper surface projection extends to the **fourth intercostal space on the right** and **fifth intercostal space on the left**
- The right adrenal gland lies beneath the peritoneal reflection near the right kidney
- The IVC is embraced in a **groove on the posterior surface** of the liver
- The anterior border lies under the right costal margin, lateral to the right rectus abdominis muscle

## Retrohepatic Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)

- The IVC runs to the right of the aorta on the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae
- Below the liver, it lies behind the duodenum and head of the pancreas
- Passes upward behind the foramen of Winslow, posterior to right hilar structures
- **Renal veins** lie in front of the arteries and join the IVC at almost a right angle
- The IVC comes to lie on the right crus of the diaphragm, behind the bare area
- Pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of **T8**

**Key surgical note:** The ligament of the vena cava must be divided to expose the IVC and right hepatic vein.

## Hepatic Veins: Overview

- The hepatic veins drain directly from the upper part of the posterior surface of the liver at an oblique angle into the IVC
- **Three major hepatic veins:**
  - **Right hepatic vein (RHV)** — largest, short extrahepatic course (~1–2 cm)
  - **Middle hepatic vein (MHV)** — runs in main portal scissura
  - **Left hepatic vein (LHV)** — usually joins MHV to form common channel
- **Umbilical vein**: single in most patients, runs beneath falciform ligament, empties into LHV
- In ~15% of patients, an **accessory right hepatic vein** is present inferiorly
- Caudate lobe drains **directly into the IVC**

## Hepatic Veins: Anatomic Relationships

- The left and middle hepatic veins may drain separately or join to form a **common venous channel** (~2 cm length)
- This common channel traverses to the left part of the anterior surface of the IVC below the diaphragm
- Hepatic venous drainage of the caudate lobe is unique — drains directly into the IVC
- The hepatic veins run between the portal sectors (sections) in the portal scissurae

## Functional Surgical Anatomy: Internal Architecture

- The internal architecture consists of **segments** that combine to form **sectors** separated by scissurae
- The scissurae contain the hepatic veins
- This functional anatomy is essential for precise hepatectomy

**Key historical contributions:**
- Couinaud (1957) — segmental classification
- Goldsmith and Woodburne (1957) — sector terminology
- McIndoe and Counseller (1927), Ton That Tung (1939), Hjortsjö (1931)
- Healey and Schroy (1953), Bismuth and colleagues (1982)

## Portal Scissurae and Sectors

- **Three main hepatic veins** within the scissurae divide the liver into **four sectors**
- Each sector receives a **portal pedicle** (portal vein branch, hepatic artery branch, bile duct)

**The main portal scissura (Cantlie's line):**
- Contains the middle hepatic vein
- Progresses from middle of gallbladder bed to left of IVC posteriorly
- Divides liver into **right liver** and **left liver** (independent vascularization and biliary drainage)

**Important:** Prefer "right liver" and "left liver" rather than "right lobe" and "left lobe"

## Right and Left Portal Scissurae

**Right portal scissura:**
- Separates right liver into **anteromedial (anterior)** and **posterolateral (posterior)** sections
- With body supine, this scissura is almost in the frontal plane
- The right hepatic vein runs within this scissura

**Left portal scissura:**
- Divides left liver into two sections
- **Not** within the umbilical fissure (which contains a portal pedicle, not a hepatic vein)
- Located posterior to the ligamentum teres, along the course of the left hepatic vein

## Couinaud's Segmental Classification

The liver is divided into **8 segments** (I–VIII):

| Segment | Location |
|---------|----------|
| I | Caudate lobe |
| II | Left lateral superior |
| III | Left lateral inferior |
| IVa | Left medial superior |
| IVb | Left medial inferior |
| V | Right anterior inferior |
| VI | Right posterior inferior |
| VII | Right posterior superior |
| VIII | Right anterior superior |

## Brisbane 2000 Terminology

::: {#tbl-brisbane}
| Anatomic Term | Couinaud Segments | Surgical Resection |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Right hemiliver/Right liver | 5–8 | Right hepatectomy |
| Left hemiliver/Left liver | 2–4 | Left hepatectomy |
| Right anterior section | 5, 8 | Right anterior sectionectomy |
| Right posterior section | 6, 7 | Right posterior sectionectomy |
| Left medial section | 4 | Left medial sectionectomy |
| Left lateral section | 2, 3 | Left lateral sectionectomy |
|  | 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 | Right trisectionectomy |
|  | 2, 3, 4, 5, 8 | Left trisectionectomy |
:::

## Portal Vein Branching at the Hilum

**Right portal triad:**
- Pursues a short course (~1–1.5 cm) before entering right liver substance
- In some cases, right anterior and posterior pedicles arise independently (separated by ~2 cm)

**Left portal triad:**
- Crosses over ~3–4 cm beneath segment IV
- Embraced in peritoneal sheath at upper end of gastrohepatic ligament
- Separated from segment IV by connective tissue (**hilar plate**)
- Turns anteriorly and caudally within umbilical fissure
- Gives branches to segment II, then III, and recurrent branches to segment IV

## Left Portal Vein Anatomy

- The left portal vein has a **longer horizontal course** within the hilar plate
- At the base of the umbilical fissure, joined by the left branch of the hepatic artery
- The umbilical portion gives branches to left hepatic segments (2 to 4)
- The left hepatic duct is located **above** the left branch of the portal vein

## Caudate Lobe (Segment I)

- The **caudate lobe** is the dorsal portion of the liver lying posteriorly
- Embraces the retrohepatic IVC
- Has a **constantly present left portion** and a **right portion of variable size**

**Key relationships:**
- Left: between IVC posteriorly and left portal triad inferiorly; middle and left hepatic veins superiorly
- Right: adjacent to segment VII (segment IX of little practical significance)
- Anterior surface: covered by posterior surface of segment IV

## Caudate Lobe: Blood Supply and Drainage

**Blood supply:**
- Supplied by vessels from **both right and left portal triads**
- Right portion (including caudate process): predominantly from right portal vein
- Left portion: from left branch of portal vein almost exclusively

**Biliary drainage:**
- Multiple small ducts drain into both right and left hepatic ducts
- In 78% of cases, drainage is into both systems
- In 15%, drainage is left hepatic ductal system only
- In 7%, drainage is into right hepatic system

**Venous drainage:**
- Unique: drains **directly into the IVC**
- Short hepatic veins drain into anterior and left aspect of vena cava
- In up to 50% of patients, caudate may completely encircle the IVC

## Caudate Lobe: Surgical Considerations

- The caudal margin can have a **papillary projection** (bulky in 27% of cases)
- May be mistaken for an enlarged lymph node on CT scan
- Posterior edge has a **fibrous component** (venal caval ligament)
- In up to 50% of patients, this ligament is replaced by hepatic tissue
- A significant **retrocaval component** may prevent left-sided approach to caudate veins

## Segmental Anatomy: Summary Points

1. The liver is divided into **two hemilivers** by the main hepatic scissura (middle hepatic vein/Cantlie's line)
2. The **left liver** is divided into: left lateral section (segments II, III) and left medial section (segment IV)
3. The **right liver** is divided into: anterior section (segments V, VIII) and posterior section (segments VI, VII)
4. **Segment I** (caudate lobe) lies posteriorly and embraces the IVC

## Intrahepatic Bile Duct Anatomy: Overview

- Right and left livers are drained by right and left hepatic ducts
- Caudate lobe drains by several ducts joining both systems
- Intrahepatic ducts are tributaries of corresponding hepatic ducts
- Bile ducts usually located **above** corresponding portal branches
- Hepatic arterial branches situated **inferiorly** to the veins

## Left Hepatic Duct System

- Drains segments II, III, and IV
- **Segment III duct**: located slightly behind left horn of umbilical recess
- Joined by tributary from segment IVb to form left duct
- Similarly joined by ducts of segment II and segment IVa
- Traverses beneath left liver at base of segment IV
- Crosses anterior edge of left portal vein
- Joins right hepatic duct to constitute hepatic ductal confluence

## Right Hepatic Duct System

- Drains segments V, VI, VII, and VIII
- Arises from junction of two main sectional duct tributaries:

**Right posterior (lateral) sectional duct:**
- Horizontal course
- Constitutes confluence of ducts of segments VI and VII

**Right anterior (medial) sectional duct:**
- Vertical descent
- Formed by confluence of ducts draining segments V and VIII
- Located to the left of corresponding portal vein branch

## Surgical Implications and Exposure

- All partial hepatectomy methods depend on control of:
  - **Inflow vasculature** and draining bile ducts
  - **Outflow hepatic veins**
- Remnant liver must have excellent:
  - Portal venous inflow
  - Hepatic arterial supply
  - Biliary drainage
  - Unimpeded hepatic venous outflow


## Biliary Tract: Introduction

- Biliary exposure and precise dissection are the **most important steps** in any biliary operative procedure
- Thorough understanding of biliary anatomy is essential
- Wide variations exist and must be recognized

## Extrahepatic Biliary Anatomy

- Extrahepatic bile ducts = extrahepatic segments of right and left hepatic ducts
- Join to form **biliary confluence**, then main biliary channel draining to duodenum
- Confluence occurs at right of hilar fissure, **anterior to portal venous bifurcation**
- Extrahepatic segment of right duct is **short**
- Extrahepatic segment of left duct has **much longer course**
- Biliary confluence separated from segment IVB by the **hilar plate**

## The Plate System

Fusion of Glisson capsule with connective tissue sheaths surrounding biliary and vascular elements:

1. **Hilar plate** — above the biliary confluence
2. **Cystic plate** — related to the gallbladder
3. **Umbilical plate** — above umbilical portion of left portal vein

**Surgical significance:**
- Possible to open the hilar plate and elevate it to display biliary confluence and left hepatic duct
- Technique called "lowering of the hilar plate"

## Main Bile Duct and Sphincter of Oddi

**Common hepatic duct:**
- Mean diameter ~6 mm
- Upper portion above cystic duct insertion

**Common bile duct (CBD):**
- Formed by union of cystic duct and common hepatic duct
- Courses downward **anterior to portal vein**, in free edge of lesser omentum
- Closely applied to hepatic artery on its left

**Sphincter of Oddi:**
- Unique cluster of smooth muscle fibers
- Distinguishable from adjacent duodenal wall smooth muscle
- CBD and pancreatic duct join within sphincter segment in 70–85% of patients

## Triangle of Calot

- **Original description:** corners = cystic duct below, cystic artery above, common hepatic duct left
- **Modern working definition:**
  - Upper border: inferior surface of right lobe of liver
  - Lower border: cystic duct
  - Other border: common hepatic duct

**Surgical significance:**
- Triangle of Calot dissection is **key during cholecystectomy**
- Cystic artery runs in this triangle
- Often the right branch of hepatic artery is found here
- Occasionally a bile duct is present and must be displayed before cholecystectomy

## Gallbladder Anatomy

- Reservoir located on undersurface of right lobe, within **cystic fossa**
- Separated from hepatic parenchyma by **cystic plate**
- Parts:
  - **Fundus** — usually reaches free edge of liver
  - **Body** — main portion
  - **Neck** — makes angle with fundus, creates **Hartmann's pouch**

**Hartmann's pouch:**
- May obscure the common hepatic duct
- Constitutes a real danger point during cholecystectomy

## Cystic Duct

- Arises from neck or infundibulum of gallbladder
- Lumen ~1–3 mm
- Length variable depending on type of union with common hepatic duct
- Mucosa arranged in **spiral folds (valves of Heister)**
- Joins common hepatic duct in supraduodenal segment in **80% of cases**
- May extend to retroduodenal or retropancreatic area
- Rarely joins right hepatic duct or right hepatic sectional duct

## Biliary Ductal Anomalies: Overview

Full knowledge of frequent variations is required for any hepatobiliary procedure.

**Normal biliary confluence** (union of right and left hepatic ducts) reported in only **72% of patients**.

Key variations include:
- Triple confluence (12%)
- Right sectional duct joins main bile duct directly (20%)
- Right sectional duct joins left hepatic duct (6%)
- Absence of hepatic duct confluence (3%)
- Right posterior duct enters cystic duct (2%)

## Hepatic Duct Confluence Variations

**Type A — Typical anatomy (57%):**
Normal confluence of right and left hepatic ducts

**Type B — Triple confluence (12%):**
Right anterior, right posterior, and left hepatic ducts meet at single point

**Type C — Ectopic drainage into common hepatic duct (16% + 4%):**
C1: Right anterior duct drains into common hepatic duct
C2: Right posterior duct drains into common hepatic duct

**Type D — Ectopic drainage into left hepatic duct (6%):**
D1: Right posterior sectional duct drains into left hepatic duct (5%)
D2: Right anterior sectional duct drains into left hepatic duct (1%)

## More Confluence Variations

**Type E — Absence of hepatic duct confluence (3%):**
E1: Separate drainage patterns
E2: Alternative arrangements

**Type F — Absence of right hepatic duct (2%):**
Right posterior duct drains into cystic duct

## Intrahepatic Bile Duct Variations

**Main right intrahepatic duct variations:**
- Ectopic drainage of segment V (9%)
- Ectopic drainage of segment VI (14%)
- Ectopic drainage of segment VIII (20%)

**Subvesical duct:**
- Described in 20–50% of cases
- Deeply embedded in cystic plate
- Joins common hepatic duct or right hepatic duct
- Does NOT drain any specific liver territory
- Does NOT communicate with gallbladder
- Injury may cause postoperative biliary leak

**Left intrahepatic variations:**
- Common union of ducts of segments III and IV (25%)
- Segment IV duct joins common hepatic duct independently (2%)

## Ectopic Drainage into Gallbladder and Cystic Duct

Main variations include:
- **A:** Cystic duct drains into biliary confluence
- **B:** Cystic duct drains into left hepatic duct (no biliary confluence)
- **C:** Segment VI duct drains into cystic duct
- **D:** Right posterior sectional duct drains into cystic duct
- **E:** Distal part of right posterior sectional duct drains into neck of gallbladder
- **F:** Proximal part of right posterior sectional duct drains into body of gallbladder

## Anomalies of the Gallbladder and Cystic Duct

**Gallbladder anomalies (rare):**
- Agenesis of gallbladder
- Bilobar gallbladders (single cystic duct, two fundi)
- Duplication of gallbladder (two cystic ducts)
- Double cystic duct draining unilocular gallbladder
- Congenital diverticulum with muscular wall

**Position anomalies:**
- **Intrahepatic position** — completely surrounded by liver tissue
- Left-sided gallbladder (rare)

## Cystic Duct Union Variations

**Mode of union with common hepatic duct:**

| Type | Frequency | Description |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| Angular union | 75% | Most frequent |
| Parallel course | 20% | Connective tissue ensheaths both ducts |
| Spiral fashion | 5% | Cystic duct approaches CBD in spiral |

- Absence of cystic duct = probably acquired anomaly (cholecystocholedochal fistula)

## Bile Duct Blood Supply

**Supraduodenal duct:**
- Blood supply is essentially **axial**
- ~8 small arteries (0.3 mm diameter) supply this segment
- Most important vessels run along lateral and medial borders = **3 o'clock and 9 o'clock arteries**
- Sources: superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, right hepatic artery branch, cystic artery, gastroduodenal artery, retroduodenal artery
- 60% run upward from major inferior vessels
- 38% run downward from right hepatic artery
- 2% nonaxial (direct from hepatic artery trunk)

**Hilar ducts:**
- Receive copious supply from surrounding vessels
- Rich network on surface of ducts

**Retropancreatic CBD:**
- Supply from retroduodenal artery
- Multiple small vessels form mural plexus

## Venous Drainage of Bile Ducts

- Veins are satellites to corresponding arteries
- Drain into 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock veins along borders of common biliary channel
- Veins draining gallbladder empty into this venous system
- NOT directly into portal vein
- Biliary tree seems to have its **own portal venous pathway to the liver**

## Biliary Exposure: Lowering the Hilar Plate

**Technique (Hepp and Couinaud):**
1. Lift segment IV upward
2. Incise Glisson capsule at its base
3. Separate upper surface of hilar plate from hepatic parenchyma
4. Display hepatic duct convergence (always extrahepatic)

**Advantages:**
- Excellent exposure of left hepatic duct (has long extrahepatic course)
- Allows mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis
- Only rarely hazardous (1% major vascular interposition)

**Limitations:**
- Less effective for exposing right hepatic duct or its branches (short extrahepatic course)
- May be difficult with atrophy/hypertrophy or deep displaced hilum

## Extended Exposure Techniques

**Simultaneous opening of:**
- Deepest portion of gallbladder fossa
- Umbilical fissure

This provides good exposure of biliary duct confluence and especially the **right hepatic duct** without full hepatotomy.

**Segment IV mobilization:**
- Incision of Glisson capsule
- Lifting segment IV upward
- Opening umbilical fissure
- Incising deepest portion of gallbladder fossa
- Particularly valuable for high bile duct strictures and liver atrophy/hypertrophy

## Umbilical Fissure and Segment III Ductal Approach

**Anatomy:**
- Round ligament (ligamentum teres) = remnant of obliterated umbilical vein
- Runs through umbilical fissure to connect with left branch of portal vein
- Sometimes deeply embedded in umbilical fissure

**Technique:**
1. Dissect round ligament on left side
2. Divide one or two vascular elongations of segment III
3. Display pedicle or anterior branch of segment III duct

**Key point:** In biliary obstruction with ductal dilation, dilated segment III duct is easily located above left branch of portal vein.

## Segment III Duct Approach: Liver Splitting

- Split liver tissue just to the left of umbilical fissure
- Widen fissure without dividing portal blood supply to segment III
- Segment III duct exposed at base of liver split
- Duct lies **above and behind** its accompanying vein
- Ready for hepaticojejunostomy

## Surgical Approaches to the Right Hepatic Biliary Ductal System

- Exposure of right intrahepatic ductal system is more hazardous and imprecise than left
- Used in critical cases of hilar cholangiocarcinoma

**Anterior sectional approach:**
1. Open liver substance through short distance in line of right anterior sectional pedicle
2. Anterior sectional duct displayed on left aspect of corresponding vein
3. Duct opened longitudinally and sewn to Roux-en-Y loop

**Alternative:** Right-sided pedicles can be encircled using technique for pedicle exposure in right-sided liver resection

## Exposure of Bile Ducts by Liver Resection

- Segment of left lobe may be amputated to expose segment II or III ducts
- Similar procedure after removal of inferior tip of right lobe
- Removal of segment IV may be carried out to expose biliary confluence
- Represents simple extension of mobilization of segment IV after opening principal scissura and umbilical fissure


## Celiac Axis and Blood Supply

**Celiac trunk:**
- Short, thick artery originating from aorta just below aortic hiatus
- Extends horizontally and forward above pancreas
- Divides into three branches:
  1. **Left gastric artery** — curves toward stomach along lesser curve
  2. **Common hepatic artery** — passes forward into retroperitoneum, curves right
  3. **Splenic artery** — largest branch, tortuous course to left

**Proper hepatic artery:**
- Continuation beyond gastroduodenal and right gastric arteries
- Usually divides into right and left branches

## Hepatic Artery: Segmental Branches

**Left hepatic artery:**
- Extends vertically toward base of umbilical fissure
- Gives off **middle hepatic artery** to segment IV
- Branch to caudate lobe
- Smaller caudate branches from left and right hepatic arteries

**Right hepatic artery:**
- Usually passes **behind** common hepatic duct
- Enters cystic triangle of Calot
- May pass in **front** of bile duct (~20% of cases)

## Hepatic Artery Variations

Classic description found in only ~60% of patients.

**Most common variations:**
- **Replaced/accessory right hepatic artery** from SMA (~25%)
  - Courses upward in groove posterolateral to CBD
  - Appears on medial side of triangle of Calot
  - Runs behind cystic duct
  
- **Replaced/accessory left hepatic artery** from left gastric artery (~25%)
  - Courses through gastrohepatic omentum
  - Enters liver at base of umbilical fissure

**Other variations:**
- Common hepatic artery from SMA
- Hepatic artery from aorta directly
- Hepatic trifurcation
- Gastroduodenal artery from right hepatic artery

## Portal Vein: Formation and Course

**Formation:**
- Formed behind neck of pancreas by confluence of **superior mesenteric vein (SMV)** and **splenic vein**
- SMV usually single trunk; may have 2–3 branches uniting beneath pancreatic neck
- Splenic vein enters from left

**Course:**
- Ascends toward liver within free edge of lesser omentum
- Lies **behind bile duct and hepatic artery**
- Surrounded by lymphatics and nodes of lesser omentum
- Receives coronary vein (communicates with esophageal venous collaterals)

## Portal Vein: Branching Pattern

- Bifurcates at liver hilus into:
  - **Larger right portal vein** — shorter length before entering liver
  - **Smaller left portal vein** — courses below left hepatic duct to enter umbilical fissure

**Right portal branch:**
- Divides at extremity of hilus into right anterior (RAS) and posterior (RPS) sectional branches

**Left portal branch:**
- Accompanied by left hepatic artery
- Branches to supply left liver segments (II–IV)
- Gives off major caudate vein before entering umbilical fissure

## Portal Vein Variations

**Trifurcation pattern (Fig. 2.40):**
- Main portal vein divides into three branches simultaneously

**Other congenital anomalies:**
- Portal vein anterior to head of pancreas and duodenum (abnormal position)
- Portal vein entering IVC directly (rare)
- Pulmonary vein entering portal vein (very rare)

**Absence of left branch of portal vein (Fig. 2.42):**
- Right branch courses through right lobe
- Curves within liver substance to supply left lobe
- Left lobe usually smaller than normal
- Associated with biliary and hepatic venous anomalies

## Portal Vein: Surgical Importance

**Critical surgical considerations:**
- Performance of right hepatic resection with division of "right portal vein" in patient with absence of left portal vein can be **fatal**
- Agenesis of right branch associated with agenesis of right hemiliver and left liver hypertrophy

**Pancreatic resection relationships:**
- Uncinate process extends behind SMV to position adjacent to SMA
- Access to portal vein behind pancreas from below
- Division of gastroduodenal artery provides greater access
- Division of CBD can provide access to right lateral aspect


## Pancreas: Overview and Position

- Posteriorly situated **retroperitoneal organ** that lies transversely
- Composed of **head, neck, body, and tail**
- Head encompassed by duodenum; tail rests in splenic hilum
- Uncinate process intimately related to SMV and SMA

**Posterior relationships:**
- IVC
- Aorta
- Left renal vein and kidney
- Spleen

**Portion lateral to portal vein:** averages 56.4% of total weight

## Pancreatic Duct System

**Duct of Wirsung (main pancreatic duct):**
- Begins in distal tail as confluence of small ductules
- Runs through body to head
- Passes downward and backward close to CBD
- Usually joins CBD within sphincter segment (70–85%)
- Enters duodenum at **papilla of Vater**, 7–10 cm distal to pylorus

**Duct of Santorini (accessory duct):**
- Runs more proximally in head of pancreas
- Usually terminates in duodenum at **accessory papilla**
- Drains body and tail of organ

## Sphincter of Oddi

- Unique cluster of smooth muscle fibers distinguishable from duodenal wall smooth muscle
- Components:
  - **Biliary sphincter** — surrounds CBD
  - **Pancreatic sphincter** — surrounds pancreatic duct
  - **Transampullary septum** — separates the two ducts
  - **Membranous septum of Boyden**
  - **Common sphincter**
- Papilla of Vater: small nipple-like structure protruding into duodenal lumen

## Pancreas Divisum

- Duct of Santorini and duct of Wirsung are **separate**
- Duct of Santorini drains mainly neck and body
- Duct of Wirsung drains mainly uncinate process portion of head
- Most common congenital anomaly of pancreatic ductal system

## Annular Pancreas

- Development of **ring of pancreatic tissue** surrounding and often embracing the duodenum
- Ring may contain a large duct and be firmly affixed to duodenal musculature
- Duodenum beneath annulus often stenosed
- Dividing ring does NOT always relieve chronic duodenal obstruction
- **Duodenojejunostomy** commonly used to relieve strictures



## Lymphatic Drainage

**Liver and gallbladder:**
- Mainly to nodes in **hepatoduodenal ligament**
- Along hepatic artery
- Gallbladder also drains via cystic node to hepatoduodenal ligament nodes and suprapancreatic nodes

**Pancreas:**
- Predominantly to nodes juxtaposed to arteries and veins
- Nodes along superior mesenteric vein
- Along borders of pancreas draining to splenic hilar nodes
- Along superior border to superior pancreatic nodes
- Celiac trunk nodes at base of common hepatic artery
- Posterior pancreaticoduodenal nodes along posterior pancreatic duodenal arterial arcade

## Nerve Supply to the Liver and Pancreas

- From branches of the **celiac ganglion**
- Composed of **sympathetic and parasympathetic** elements
- Splanchnic nerves (sympathetic) and vagal nerves (parasympathetic)
- Distributed mainly in association with major arteries

## Key Takeaways

- The liver has **dual segmentation systems**: traditional (external lobes) and functional (Couinaud's 8 segments)
- **Brisbane 2000 terminology** standardizes hepatic resection nomenclature
- Biliary anatomy has **wide variations** — only 72% have "normal" confluence
- **Hepatic artery variations** occur in ~40% of patients
- Portal vein anomalies, though rare, can be **surgically fatal** if unrecognized
- The **plate system** (hilar, cystic, umbilical) enables safe biliary exposure
- Pancreas divisum and annular pancreas are the most clinically significant pancreatic anomalies
